jurisdiction: United States federal law. This topic is legal-adjacent: every legal claim is anchored to the IDEA statute (20 U.S.C. 1400 et seq.), its implementing regulations (34 C.F.R. The lesson states plainly that it is educational material and not legal advice, and it gives no individualized guidance about any particular child, school, or dispute.

claims.claim: IDEA is United States federal law. It is a conditional-spending statute: it offers States federal funds to assist in educating children with disabilities and conditions that funding on compliance with statutory requirements, including the requirement that States provide every eligible child a free appropriate public education by means of an individualized education program.

One of IDEA's stated purposes is to ensure that all children with disabilities have available to them a free appropriate public education that emphasizes special education and related services designed to meet their unique needs and prepare them for further education, employment, and independent living.

Eligibility under IDEA Part B is a two-part test, not a diagnosis. 34 C.F.R. 300.8(a)(1) defines a child with a disability as a child evaluated as having one of the enumerated conditions 'and who, by reason thereof, needs special education and related services.' Each category definition in 300.8(c) additionally requires that the condition adversely affect educational performance. Under 300.8(a)(2), a child who needs only a related service and not special education is not a child with a disability under IDEA, unless that related service is considered special education under State standards.

34 C.F.R. 300.8(c) enumerates 13 disability categories: autism, deaf-blindness, deafness, emotional disturbance, hearing impairment, intellectual disability, multiple disabilities, orthopedic impairment, other health impairment, specific learning disability, speech or language impairment, traumatic brain injury, and visual impairment including blindness. Separately, 300.8(b) permits a State and LEA to use an optional 'developmental delay' category for children aged three through nine.

Special education means specially designed instruction, at no cost to parents, to meet the unique needs of a child with a disability. Specially designed instruction means adapting the content, methodology, or delivery of instruction to address the child's unique needs resulting from the disability and to ensure the child's access to the general curriculum. Special education is therefore defined as a service, not as a location.

IDEA Part C serves infants and toddlers with disabilities birth through age 2 and their families through early intervention services documented in an Individualized Family Service Plan; Part B serves children and youth ages 3 through 21 through special education and related services documented in an IEP.

The IFSP is family-centered in a way the IEP is not: 34 C.F.R. 303.344 requires a statement of the family's resources, priorities, and concerns related to enhancing the development of the child, requires that each early intervention service be provided in the natural environment to the maximum extent appropriate or that the record justify why it is not, and requires the name of a service coordinator.

Child find obligates States to identify, locate, and evaluate all children with disabilities residing in the State who are in need of special education and related services, including homeless children, wards of the State, and children attending private schools, regardless of the severity of their disability. It expressly reaches children suspected of having a disability and needing special education 'even though they are advancing from grade to grade,' and highly mobile children including migrant children.

Either a parent or a public agency may request an initial evaluation. The evaluation must be conducted within 60 days of receiving parental consent, or within a timeframe the State establishes if it has set one.

Evaluation must use a variety of assessment tools and strategies, and no single measure or assessment may be used as the sole criterion for determining whether a child is a child with a disability. Materials must be selected and administered so as not to be discriminatory on a racial or cultural basis and must be provided in the child's native language or other mode of communication. The child must be assessed in all areas related to the suspected disability, and the evaluation must be sufficiently comprehensive to identify all of the child's special education and related services needs, whether or not commonly linked to the disability category.

34 C.F.R. 300.306(b)(1) forbids determining that a child is a child with a disability if the determinant factor is lack of appropriate instruction in reading (including the essential components of reading instruction), lack of appropriate instruction in math, or limited English proficiency. Eligibility is determined by a group of qualified professionals and the parent of the child.

34 C.F.R. 300.320(a) requires an IEP to contain present levels of academic achievement and functional performance including how the disability affects involvement and progress in the general education curriculum; measurable annual academic and functional goals; a description of how and when progress toward those goals will be measured and reported; a statement of special education, related services, supplementary aids and services based on peer-reviewed research to the extent practicable, and program modifications or supports for school personnel; an explanation of the extent, if any, to which the child will not participate with nondisabled children; any individual accommodations for State and districtwide assessments; and the projected start date, frequency, location, and duration of services. Under 300.320(b), transition services must be included beginning not later than the first IEP to be in effect when the child turns 16, or younger if the IEP Team determines it appropriate.

The IEP Team must include the parents; not less than one regular education teacher of the child if the child is or may be participating in the regular education environment; not less than one special education teacher or provider; a representative of the public agency; an individual who can interpret the instructional implications of evaluation results; other individuals with knowledge or special expertise at the discretion of the parent or agency; and, whenever appropriate, the child.

LRE is a legal presumption toward the regular educational environment, not a placement label. To the maximum extent appropriate, children with disabilities must be educated with children who are nondisabled, and removal from the regular educational environment may occur only if the nature or severity of the disability is such that education in regular classes with the use of supplementary aids and services cannot be achieved satisfactorily.

Each public agency must ensure a continuum of alternative placements is available, including instruction in regular classes, special classes, special schools, home instruction, and instruction in hospitals and institutions, and must make provision for supplementary services such as a resource room or itinerant instruction to be provided in conjunction with regular class placement.

Placement is decided by a group including the parents, is determined at least annually, is based on the child's IEP, is as close as possible to the child's home, and unless the IEP requires otherwise the child is educated in the school he or she would attend if nondisabled. A child may not be removed from education in age-appropriate regular classrooms solely because of needed modifications in the general education curriculum.

In Board of Education of the Hendrick Hudson Central School District v. Rowley, 458 U.S. 176 (No. 80-1002, argued March 23, 1982, decided June 28, 1982), Justice Rehnquist delivered the opinion of the Court, joined by Burger, C.J., Powell, Stevens, and O'Connor; Blackmun concurred in the judgment; White dissented, joined by Brennan and Marshall. The Court held that the Act does not require a State to maximize the potential of each handicapped child commensurate with the opportunity provided nonhandicapped children, and set a two-part judicial inquiry: whether the State complied with the Act's procedures, and whether the IEP developed through those procedures is reasonably calculated to enable the child to receive educational benefits.

Rowley expressly declined to establish any one test for determining the adequacy of educational benefits conferred upon all children covered by the Act, confining its analysis to the facts before it, which involved a child progressing smoothly through the regular curriculum. For children fully integrated in the regular classroom, Rowley said the IEP should typically be reasonably calculated to enable the child to achieve passing marks and advance from grade to grade.

In Endrew F. v. Douglas County School District RE-1, 580 U.S. 386 (No. 15-827, argued January 11, 2017, decided March 22, 2017), Chief Justice Roberts delivered the opinion for a unanimous Court, holding that to meet its substantive obligation under the IDEA, a school must offer an IEP reasonably calculated to enable a child to make progress appropriate in light of the child's circumstances.

Endrew F. did not overrule Rowley. It rejected the Tenth Circuit's gloss on Rowley - that an IEP is adequate so long as it confers an educational benefit 'merely more than de minimis' - describing its own standard as 'markedly more demanding' than that test. The Court reasoned it 'cannot be the case that the Act typically aims for grade-level advancement for children with disabilities who can be educated in the regular classroom, but is satisfied with barely more than de minimis progress for those who cannot.'

Endrew F. also declined to raise the standard as far as the parents asked. The parents argued FAPE requires opportunities 'substantially equal to the opportunities afforded children without disabilities.' The Court noted this was strikingly similar to the standard the lower courts adopted in Rowley and that the Rowley majority rejected any such standard in clear terms, and declined to interpret the FAPE provision in a manner so plainly at odds with that analysis, given that Congress has not materially changed the statutory definition of FAPE since Rowley.

Under Endrew F., a child's IEP need not aim for grade-level advancement if that is not a reasonable prospect, but the child's educational program 'must be appropriately ambitious in light of his circumstances, just as advancement from grade to grade is appropriately ambitious for most children in the regular classroom,' and 'every child should have the chance to meet challenging objectives.' The Court described this as a general standard, not a formula.

Procedural safeguards include a safeguards notice covering independent educational evaluations, prior written notice, parental consent, access to education records, State complaint and due process complaint procedures, mediation, the child's placement during the pendency of a due process complaint, unilateral private placement, hearings, State-level appeals where applicable, civil actions, and attorneys' fees. The notice must generally be given once a school year, with additional copies at initial referral or parent-requested evaluation, upon receipt of the first State or due process complaint in a school year, in accordance with discipline procedures, and on parent request.

Mediation must be available for disputes under Part B, must be voluntary on the part of the parties, may not be used to deny or delay a parent's right to a due process hearing, and must be conducted by a qualified and impartial mediator trained in effective mediation techniques.

A parent or a public agency may file a due process complaint on matters relating to the identification, evaluation, or educational placement of a child with a disability, or the provision of FAPE. The complaint must allege a violation that occurred not more than two years before the date the parent or public agency knew or should have known about the alleged action, subject to stated exceptions.

Under the stay-put provision, during the pendency of any administrative or judicial proceeding regarding a due process complaint, unless the agency and parents agree otherwise, the child must remain in his or her current educational placement.

Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act uses a functional, non-categorical definition of disability: a physical or mental impairment that substantially limits one or more major life activities, plus the record-of and regarded-as prongs. Major life activities include caring for oneself, performing manual tasks, walking, seeing, hearing, speaking, breathing, learning, working, eating, sleeping, reading, concentrating, thinking, and communicating. A student may be eligible for services under Section 504 without being eligible under IDEA, receiving adjustments in the regular classroom rather than special education. Under the Section 504 regulations, implementing an IEP is one way to meet the Section 504 FAPE requirement.

IDEA itself addresses racial and ethnic disparity. 20 U.S.C. 1418(d) and 34 C.F.R. 300.646 require each State to determine whether significant disproportionality based on race and ethnicity is occurring in the identification of children as children with disabilities including identification by particular impairment, in placement in particular educational settings, and in the incidence, duration, and type of disciplinary removals including suspensions and expulsions.

When significant disproportionality is identified, the State must provide for review and, if appropriate, revision of the policies, practices, and procedures used in identification or placement; must require the LEA to reserve the maximum amount of early intervening services funds to provide comprehensive coordinated early intervening services; and must require the LEA to publicly report on the revision of policies, practices, and procedures. The early intervening services reservation is capped at 15 percent of the LEA's Part B funds under 34 C.F.R. 300.226(a), and comprehensive coordinated early intervening services may serve children from age 3 through grade 12 with and without disabilities.

34 C.F.R. 300.647 requires States to use a standard methodology - a risk ratio, or an alternate risk ratio when comparison-group data are insufficient - calculated for seven racial and ethnic groups, with each State setting a reasonable risk ratio threshold, minimum cell size, and minimum n-size.

In school year 2022-23, 7.5 million students ages 3 through 21 received special education and/or related services under IDEA, equal to 15 percent of all U.S. public school students. The largest categories were specific learning disabilities (32 percent of those served), speech or language impairments (19 percent), other health impairments (15 percent), autism (13 percent), developmental delay (7 percent), intellectual disability (6 percent), and emotional disturbance (4 percent).

The U.S. Department of Education's IDEA site states that more than 8 million eligible infants, toddlers, children, and youth with disabilities were served as of school year 2022-23, including more than 441,000 infants and toddlers under Part C. This total is broader than the NCES figure of 7.5 million students ages 3 through 21, because it spans Part C and Part B rather than Part B alone.

In fall 2022, 95 percent of students ages 5 through 21 served under IDEA were enrolled in regular schools, and 67 percent of those students spent 80 percent or more of their time in general classes, up from 61 percent in fall 2012. That share varies sharply by category: 89 percent for students with speech or language impairments and 21 percent for students with intellectual disabilities.

Rates of being served under IDEA differ by race and ethnicity in the aggregate. In school year 2022-23 the percentage of public school students served was highest for American Indian/Alaska Native students (19 percent) and Black students (17 percent), and lowest for Asian students (8 percent) and Pacific Islander students (12 percent), with White (15 percent) and Hispanic (14 percent) students in between.

Whether aggregate racial disparity in identification reflects over-identification of students of color is genuinely contested in the research literature. A National Research Council committee reviewed disproportionate representation in 2002 and examined contributors including early biological and environmental influences, unequal opportunity, and possible bias in referral and assessment. Morgan and colleagues (2015), analyzing longitudinal data and adjusting for individual student characteristics including achievement and family income, reported that minority children were consistently less likely than otherwise similar White, English-speaking children to be identified as disabled. That paper drew published rebuttals in the same and other journals.

Section 504 and Title II of the ADA have different jurisdictional hooks. ED's Office for Civil Rights enforces both in education and states that Section 504 applies to recipients of Federal financial assistance while Title II applies to public entities. The ADA applies to state and local governments even if they are small or receive federal money, so Title II coverage of a public school does not depend on federal funding.

The ADA defines a person with a disability as someone who has a physical or mental impairment that substantially limits one or more major life activities, has a history or record of such an impairment, or is perceived by others as having such an impairment. Title II covers all services, programs, and activities of state and local governments including public education; Title III covers businesses and nonprofits serving the public.

The 'six principles of IDEA' framing (FAPE, appropriate evaluation, IEP, LRE, parent and student participation, procedural safeguards) is a widely taught organizing device used by parent centers and teacher-preparation materials, not a numbered enumeration appearing in the statute. Each principle corresponds to obligations located in separate provisions of 20 U.S.C. 1400 et seq. and 34 C.F.R. Part 300.

positions: Popular summaries and some professional-development materials describe Endrew F. as replacing or overturning Rowley's FAPE standard.

The opinion itself treats Rowley as controlling and instructive, states that 'Rowley and the language of the IDEA point to the approach adopted here,' and rejects the parents' proposed higher standard precisely because the Rowley majority rejected a strikingly similar one.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the accurate relationship. Endrew F. did not overrule Rowley; it built on Rowley and rejected a lower-court reading of Rowley - the Tenth Circuit's 'merely more than de minimis' gloss - as too low, while simultaneously declining to adopt the substantially-equal-opportunity standard the parents sought. Verified against the U.S. Reports text of both opinions, not against secondary summaries.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Who wrote Rowley and what was the vote?
positions: One retrieved summary of the U.S. Reports PDF asserted the opinion was delivered by Justice White for a unanimous Court, argued December 5, 1981.

The U.S. Reports text itself states: 'Rehnquist, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Burger, C. J., and Powell, Stevens, and O'Connor, JJ., joined. Blackmun, J., filed an opinion concurring in the judgment. White, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Brennan and Marshall, JJ., joined.' Argued March 23, 1982, decided June 28, 1982.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The automated summary was wrong on author, vote, and argument date. The lesson uses the U.S. Reports text, extracted and read directly. This is recorded here because it is exactly the kind of error a legal topic must not inherit from a secondary summary.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How many people does IDEA serve?
positions: NCES reports 7.5 million students ages 3-21 served under IDEA in school year 2022-23, 15 percent of public school enrollment.
ED's IDEA site states more than 8 million eligible infants, toddlers, children, and youth as of school year 2022-23.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: These are different populations, not conflicting counts. The NCES figure covers Part B (ages 3-21); ED's figure spans Part C (birth through 2, more than 441,000 in 2022-23) and Part B together. The lesson gives both with their scope and school year attached, and does not present either as a single undated headline number.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Does aggregate racial disparity in IDEA identification demonstrate over-identification of students of color?
positions: Descriptive federal data show higher rates of being served under IDEA for American Indian/Alaska Native and Black students than for White, Hispanic, and Asian students, and a long research and policy literature - including the 2002 National Research Council report - treats disproportionate representation as a serious equity problem with plausible contributors in referral and assessment.

Morgan et al. (2015) found that after adjusting for individual-level characteristics such as prior achievement and family income, minority children were less likely than otherwise similar White, English-speaking children to be identified as disabled, implying under-identification rather than over-identification.
Published responses argued that this framing oversimplifies educational inequity and that conditioning on achievement conditions on an outcome shaped by the same inequities.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson reports the descriptive federal figures as descriptive, states plainly that the causal interpretation is contested and why the two literatures reach different conclusions, and separates the empirical dispute from the legal fact that IDEA contains significant disproportionality provisions States must apply regardless. It does not adjudicate the research dispute.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Is the 'six principles of IDEA' framing statutory?
positions: Parent centers, teacher-preparation texts, and state agencies commonly teach six principles: FAPE, appropriate evaluation, IEP, LRE, parent and student participation, and procedural safeguards.

No provision of 20 U.S.C. 1400 et seq. enumerates six numbered principles under that heading; the frame is a teaching device that organizes obligations located in different parts of the statute and regulations.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the six-principle frame because it is the vocabulary students will meet, but says explicitly that it is an organizing device rather than a statutory list, and anchors each principle to the specific statutory or regulatory provision that actually creates the obligation.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Are all IDEA-eligible students automatically covered by Section 504?
positions: Many secondary explainers state flatly that every student eligible under IDEA is automatically protected by Section 504 and Title II of the ADA.

ED's Office for Civil Rights FAQ establishes the converse direction - that a student may be eligible under Section 504 without needing special education under IDEA - and states that implementing an IEP is one way to meet the Section 504 FAPE requirement. It does not assert automatic 504 coverage for every IDEA-eligible student, and the two statutes use different eligibility definitions applied individually.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson was corrected during fact-check. It no longer claims that every IDEA-eligible student is automatically a Section 504 student. It states the direction the source actually supports - that Section 504 reaches students IDEA does not - notes that in practice IDEA-eligible students will typically also meet Section 504's functional definition, and flags that each statute's eligibility is determined under its own standard.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft contained no substantive claims about special education at all. Its In 30 Seconds, Why It Matters, College Version, vocabulary, Eli-10, worked example, common mistakes, key takeaway, and all three quick-check questions were topic-agnostic boilerplate with the topic title substituted in ('Special Education Foundations is a foundational concept in Education'). None of it was verifiable because none of it asserted anything about IDEA, FAPE, IEPs, LRE, eligibility, or disability law.

The draft's vocabulary defined 'Special Education Foundations' circularly as 'A foundational Education concept covered in this lesson,' and defined three generic words (context, evidence, application) that are not terms of art in this topic.
The draft carried an empty sources array while presenting substantive-sounding assertions.
The draft's analogy ('a label on a toolbox drawer') was generic boilerplate flagged by the acceptance gate and had no connection to special education law.

Supplies the ordering rule that services are decided before placement.

sourceRecords.title: 34 C.F.R. 300.301 - Initial evaluations
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Department of Education, Office of Special Education Programs (IDEA regulations site)
sourceRecords.notes: Used for the rule that either a parent or a public agency may initiate a request for an initial evaluation, for the parental consent requirement cross-referenced to 300.300, and for the 60-day timeline in (c)(1) running from receipt of parental consent, subject to a State-established timeframe where one exists.

sourceRecords.title: 34 C.F.R. 300.304 - Evaluation procedures
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Department of Education, Office of Special Education Programs (IDEA regulations site)
sourceRecords.notes: Used for (b)(1) requiring a variety of assessment tools and strategies; (b)(2) prohibiting any single measure or assessment as the sole criterion for determining disability; (c)(1) requiring that materials not be discriminatory on a racial or cultural basis and be administered in the child's native language or other mode of communication; (c)(4) requiring assessment in all areas related to the suspected disability; and (c)(6) requiring the evaluation to be sufficiently comprehensive to identify all special education and related services needs whether or not commonly linked to the disability category.

sourceRecords.title: 34 C.F.R. 300.306 - Determination of eligibility
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Department of Education, Office of Special Education Programs (IDEA regulations site)
sourceRecords.notes: Used for (a)(1), under which a group of qualified professionals and the parent of the child determine eligibility, and for the special rule at (b)(1) barring a disability determination where the determinant factor is lack of appropriate instruction in reading including the essential components of reading instruction, lack of appropriate instruction in math, or limited English proficiency. This is the authority for the lesson's point that instructional failure and language acquisition must be ruled out before eligibility is found.

sourceRecords.title: 34 C.F.R. 300.320 - Definition of individualized education program
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Department of Education, Office of Special Education Programs (IDEA regulations site)
sourceRecords.notes: Used for the required contents of an IEP at (a)(1)-(a)(7): present levels of academic achievement and functional performance including the effect of the disability on involvement and progress in the general education curriculum; measurable annual academic and functional goals; how and when progress will be measured and reported; special education, related services, supplementary aids and services based on peer-reviewed research to the extent practicable, and program modifications or supports for school personnel; an explanation of the extent, if any, to which the child will not participate with nondisabled children; accommodations for State and districtwide assessments; and projected start date, frequency, location, and duration. Also used for (b), transition services beginning not later than the first IEP in effect when the child turns 16, or younger if the Team determines it appropriate.

sourceRecords.title: 34 C.F.R. 300.321 - IEP Team
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Department of Education, Office of Special Education Programs (IDEA regulations site)
sourceRecords.notes: Used for required IEP Team membership at (a): the parents; not less than one regular education teacher of the child if the child is or may be participating in the regular education environment; not less than one special education teacher or provider; a representative of the public agency qualified to provide or supervise specially designed instruction and knowledgeable about the general education curriculum and agency resources; an individual who can interpret the instructional implications of evaluation results; other individuals with knowledge or special expertise at the discretion of the parent or agency; and, whenever appropriate, the child. Supports the lesson's treatment of parent participation as a structural requirement rather than a courtesy.

sourceRecords.title: 34 C.F.R. 300.504 - Procedural safeguards notice
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Department of Education, Office of Special Education Programs (IDEA regulations site)
sourceRecords.notes: Used for when the safeguards notice must be given (generally once a school year, plus at initial referral or parent-requested evaluation, on receipt of the first State or due process complaint in a school year, in accordance with the discipline procedures, and on parent request) and for the full list of safeguards the notice must explain, including independent educational evaluations, prior written notice, parental consent, access to education records, State and due process complaint procedures, mediation, placement during pendency, unilateral private placement, hearings, State-level appeals, civil actions, and attorneys' fees.

sourceRecords.title: 34 C.F.R. 300.506 - Mediation
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Department of Education, Office of Special Education Programs (IDEA regulations site)
sourceRecords.notes: Used for the requirements that mediation be available for any matter under Part B, be voluntary on the part of the parties, not be used to deny or delay a parent's right to a due process hearing or any other right, and be conducted by a qualified and impartial mediator trained in effective mediation techniques.

sourceRecords.title: 34 C.F.R. 300.507 - Filing a due process complaint
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Department of Education, Office of Special Education Programs (IDEA regulations site)
sourceRecords.notes: Used for who may file (a parent or a public agency), the subject matter (identification, evaluation, or educational placement of a child with a disability, or the provision of FAPE), and the two-year limitation running from when the party knew or should have known about the alleged action, subject to exceptions.

sourceRecords.title: 34 C.F.R. 300.518 - Child's status during proceedings
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Department of Education, Office of Special Education Programs (IDEA regulations site)
sourceRecords.notes: Used for the stay-put rule: during the pendency of any administrative or judicial proceeding regarding a due process complaint, unless the agency and parents agree otherwise, the child must remain in his or her current educational placement. Used in the lesson to show that procedural safeguards have substantive consequences during a dispute.

sourceRecords.title: 34 C.F.R. 300.646 - Disproportionality
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Department of Education, Office of Special Education Programs (IDEA regulations site)
sourceRecords.notes: Used for the State duty to determine significant disproportionality based on race and ethnicity with respect to identification (overall and by particular impairment), placement in particular educational settings, and the incidence, duration, and type of disciplinary removals including suspensions and expulsions; and for the consequences - annual review and revision of policies, practices, and procedures, reservation of the maximum early intervening services funds for comprehensive coordinated early intervening services, and public reporting. Also used for the rule that an LEA may not limit comprehensive coordinated early intervening services to children with disabilities and may serve children from age 3 through grade 12.

sourceRecords.title: 34 C.F.R. 300.647 - Determining significant disproportionality
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Department of Education, Office of Special Education Programs (IDEA regulations site)
sourceRecords.notes: Used for the standard methodology States must apply: a risk ratio comparing the risk of an outcome for one racial or ethnic group in an LEA against the risk for all other groups in that LEA, or an alternate risk ratio using the State comparison group when LEA comparison data are insufficient; the seven racial and ethnic groups analyzed; the outcome categories analyzed for identification, placement, and discipline; and each State's obligation to set a reasonable risk ratio threshold, minimum cell size, and minimum n-size.

sourceRecords.title: 34 C.F.R. 303.344 - Content of an IFSP
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Department of Education, Office of Special Education Programs (IDEA Part C regulations site)
sourceRecords.notes: Used for the contents of the Individualized Family Service Plan under Part C: present levels of physical, cognitive, communication, social or emotional, and adaptive development; a statement of the family's resources, priorities, and concerns related to enhancing the development of the child; measurable results or outcomes for child and family; early intervention services based on peer-reviewed research to the extent practicable with length, duration, frequency, intensity, and method of delivery; the natural environments statement or justification; a named service coordinator; and steps supporting transition out of Part C. Supplies the concrete basis for the lesson's IFSP-versus-IEP contrast.

sourceRecords.title: Board of Education of the Hendrick Hudson Central School District, Westchester County v. Rowley, 458 U.S. 176 (1982)
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Government Publishing Office, United States Reports volume 458
sourceRecords.notes: The official U.S. Reports text, downloaded and read directly rather than summarized. Used for: No. 80-1002, argued March 23, 1982, decided June 28, 1982; the lineup - Rehnquist, J., delivered the opinion, joined by Burger, C.J., Powell, Stevens, and O'Connor, with Blackmun concurring in the judgment and White dissenting joined by Brennan and Marshall; the holding that the Act does not require a State to maximize the potential of each handicapped child commensurate with the opportunity provided nonhandicapped children; the two-part judicial inquiry into procedural compliance and whether the IEP is reasonably calculated to enable the child to receive educational benefits; and the statement that for a child educated in regular classrooms the IEP should be reasonably calculated to enable the child to achieve passing marks and advance from grade to grade. Reading the primary text corrected an automated summary that misreported the author, the vote, and the argument date. Court opinions are government edicts and are not copyrightable.

sourceRecords.title: Endrew F. v. Douglas County School District RE-1, 580 U.S. 386 (2017)
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Government Publishing Office, United States Reports volume 580
sourceRecords.notes: The official U.S. Reports text, downloaded and read directly. Used for: No. 15-827, argued January 11, 2017, decided March 22, 2017, Roberts, C.J., delivering the opinion for a unanimous Court, vacating and remanding 798 F.3d 1329; the holding that to meet its substantive obligation a school must offer an IEP reasonably calculated to enable a child to make progress appropriate in light of the child's circumstances; the characterization of that standard as 'markedly more demanding' than the Tenth Circuit's 'merely more than de minimis' test; the reasoning that it cannot be the case that the Act aims for grade-level advancement for children who can be educated in the regular classroom but is satisfied with barely more than de minimis progress for those who cannot; the 'appropriately ambitious' and 'challenging objectives' passage for children not able to achieve on grade level; the acknowledgment that this is a general standard, not a formula; and the Court's rejection of the parents' proposed 'substantially equal' opportunity standard because the Rowley majority had rejected a strikingly similar one. Also used to establish that Rowley declined to establish any one test and confined its analysis, which is how the lesson explains that Endrew F. built on Rowley rather than overruling it.

sourceRecords.title: Questions and Answers on U.S. Supreme Court Case Decision Endrew F. v. Douglas County School District Re-1 (December 7, 2017)
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Department of Education, Office of Special Education and Rehabilitative Services
sourceRecords.notes: The Department's own guidance on Endrew F., dated December 7, 2017. Used as corroboration that the Department reads the decision as rejecting the merely-more-than-de-minimis standard, as applying to students performing at grade level and to students unable to achieve grade-level performance alike, and as requiring individualized rather than uniform progress expectations. Reuse terms are not stated for the page text, so it is recorded reference only and its wording was not adapted; the lesson's legal statements rest on the opinion itself.

sourceRecords.title: About IDEA
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Department of Education, Office of Special Education Programs
sourceRecords.notes: Existing registry source, reused with its registered URL unchanged. Used here for the Part C and Part B division - infants and toddlers birth through age 2 receiving early intervention services, children and youth ages 3 through 21 receiving special education and related services - for the original 1975 enactment as the Education for All Handicapped Children Act and the most recent amendment through Public Law 114-95 in December 2015, and for the Department's statement that more than 8 million eligible infants, toddlers, children, and youth were served as of school year 2022-23, including more than 441,000 infants and toddlers under Part C. Reuse terms are not stated for page text, so it remains reference only.

sourceRecords.title: Frequently Asked Questions: Section 504 and Free Appropriate Public Education (FAPE)
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Department of Education, Office for Civil Rights
sourceRecords.notes: The Office for Civil Rights FAQ. Used for Section 504's functional three-prong definition of disability (a physical or mental impairment substantially limiting one or more major life activities, a record of such an impairment, or being regarded as having one), for the illustrative list of major life activities, for the point that a student may be eligible for services under Section 504 without needing special education under IDEA and may instead receive adjustments in the regular classroom, for Section 504's FAPE formulation as regular or special education and related aids and services designed to meet the student's individual educational needs as adequately as the needs of nondisabled students are met, and for the statement that implementing an IEP is one way to meet the Section 504 FAPE requirement. This is the primary basis for the lesson's IDEA-versus-504 comparison. Reuse terms are not stated for page text, so it is recorded reference only.

sourceRecords.title: Condition of Education: Students With Disabilities (last updated May 2024)
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Statistics
sourceRecords.notes: Checked live on 2026-08-18; the most recent data year on the indicator is school year 2022-23 and the page is marked last updated May 2024, so the lesson dates the figures rather than presenting them as current-year. Used for 7.5 million students ages 3-21 served under IDEA in 2022-23, equal to 15 percent of all public school students; for the category distribution (specific learning disabilities 32 percent, speech or language impairments 19 percent, other health impairments 15 percent, autism 13 percent, developmental delay 7 percent, intellectual disability 6 percent, emotional disturbance 4 percent); and for the percentage of public school students served by race and ethnicity (American Indian/Alaska Native 19, Black 17, White 15, Hispanic 14, Pacific Islander 12, Asian 8). Figures and their attribution were taken; the page's prose was not adapted.

sourceRecords.title: Fast Facts: Inclusion of Students With Disabilities (indicator 59)
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Statistics
sourceRecords.notes: Used for fall 2022 placement data: 95 percent of students ages 5-21 served under IDEA were enrolled in regular schools, 2 percent in separate schools for students with disabilities, 2 percent parentally placed in private schools, and 1 percent homebound, hospitalized, or in other facilities; 67 percent of those in regular schools spent 80 percent or more of their time in general classes, up from 61 percent in fall 2012; and the spread across categories, from 89 percent for speech or language impairments to 21 percent for intellectual disabilities. These figures give the lesson's LRE section an empirical anchor showing that the continuum is genuinely used and used unevenly.

sourceRecords.title: Minority Students in Special and Gifted Education (2002)
sourceRecords.provider: Committee on Minority Representation in Special Education, National Research Council of the National Academies; National Academies Press
sourceRecords.notes: Consensus study report of a National Research Council committee convened at the request of the Office for Civil Rights. Used for the existence and framing of the disproportionate-representation problem and for the range of contributors the committee examined - early biological and environmental influences, inequities in preschool and K-12 opportunity, and possible bias in the referral and assessment system - and for the point that racial and ethnic disproportion in gifted and talented programs generally runs in the opposite direction. Cited to establish that this is a long-standing, seriously studied question, not to settle it. Copyrighted; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Minorities Are Disproportionately Underrepresented in Special Education: Longitudinal Evidence Across Five Disability Conditions (Educational Researcher, 44(5), 278-292)
sourceRecords.provider: Morgan, Farkas, Hillemeier, Mattison, Maczuga, Li, and Cook; American Educational Research Association (ERIC record EJ1068118)
sourceRecords.notes: Used for the counter-finding that after adjusting for individual-level characteristics including prior achievement and family income, racial and ethnic minority children from kindergarten entry through the end of middle school were consistently less likely than otherwise similar White, English-speaking children to be identified as having learning disabilities, speech or language impairments, intellectual disabilities, health impairments, or emotional disturbances. Cited alongside the published rebuttals it drew, to show the lesson's readers that the causal interpretation of aggregate disparity is contested rather than settled. Copyrighted; cited for findings only, no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Disability Discrimination: Laws OCR Enforces in Education
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Department of Education, Office for Civil Rights
sourceRecords.notes: Used for the jurisdictional hook that distinguishes the two civil rights statutes in education: OCR enforces Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 and Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990; Section 504 applies to recipients of Federal financial assistance, while Title II applies to public entities. This supplies the sourcing for the lesson's Section 504 versus ADA Title II comparison, which previously rested on general knowledge.

sourceRecords.title: Introduction to the ADA and Title II of the ADA (State and Local Governments)
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Rights Division (ADA.gov)
sourceRecords.notes: Used for the ADA's three-prong definition of disability (a physical or mental impairment that substantially limits one or more major life activities, a history or record of such an impairment, or being perceived by others as having one); for Title II covering all services, programs, and activities of state and local governments including public education, while Title III covers businesses and nonprofits serving the public; and for the statement that the ADA applies to state and local governments even if small or receiving federal money, confirming Title II coverage does not turn on federal funding. Companion page https://www.ada.gov/topics/title-ii/ was also read and states that Title II requires state and local governments to give people with disabilities an equal opportunity to benefit from all their programs, services, and activities, listing public education among them.
